messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 51
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: School Principal
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell, Medical Procedures: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction, Isolate Completely: cut off all contact with friends and family, Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
  Memory: Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
  Negative Appraisals: Unrecognisable Self: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Clinical Vignette: Marcus

Marcus was fifty-one when the diagnosis came through—stage three lymphoma, discovered during a routine physical he'd almost skipped. He remembered the oncologist's voice, the smell of that examination room, the way his hands had trembled as he signed consent forms for chemotherapy. He'd survived eighteen months of treatment: the port in his chest, the chemicals burning through his veins, the hospital smell that became the smell of his own mortality. His wife Sarah had held his hand through most of it. Two years after remission, she died in a car accident on a Tuesday afternoon. Marcus had been at work, principal of Lincoln Elementary, when the police called. He'd never made it to the hospital in time to say goodbye.

The first months after Sarah's death were numb. But by autumn, something had shifted. Walking past the hospital on his drive home from school, Marcus felt his chest tighten, his breathing shallow. The smell—that particular antiseptic tang that drifted through the parking lot—sent him spiraling. He couldn't name what he was afraid of anymore. The cancer was gone. Sarah was gone. But his body seemed to remember something his mind couldn't quite grasp, a sensation of paralysis and dread that arrived without warning whenever he caught that hospital smell or, worse, when someone mentioned needing blood work. The feeling came as pure terror, sometimes without any clear image—just the overwhelming sense that he was dying, that his body was betraying him again.

Marcus had come to believe that he could no longer trust himself. He'd survived cancer; he'd failed to reach Sarah in time. The person he'd been before—the steady principal, the man who made decisions, who led a school—felt like someone else entirely. Now, any unexpected demand triggered an elaborate defense: he began rehearsing conversations before meetings, scripting his words so carefully that colleagues noticed his stilted responses. When the school nurse mentioned scheduling a health screening, Marcus felt the familiar surge of panic, and he simply didn't show up. He began avoiding the hospital entirely, taking longer routes home, refusing to drive past it. The avoidance made him feel safer momentarily, but it also deepened his conviction that something was fundamentally wrong with him. He was weak. He couldn't rely on his own judgment anymore.

By spring, Marcus had begun isolating. Invitations from friends went unanswered. He'd rehearse reasons to decline dinner, practice the exact words he'd use to keep people at arm's length. His sister called repeatedly; he let the calls go to voicemail. The isolation fed his sense of being unreliable—if he couldn't show up for the people who cared about him, what kind of man was he? Meanwhile, whenever his mind drifted toward those eighteen months of treatment, or toward the day Sarah died, the memories came fragmented and strange. He'd feel his body hunching forward, the way he had in the chemo chair, without any accompanying image. Other times, the full weight of the hospital room would crash over him—the smell, the cold metal of the examination table, the certainty that he was going to die—yet when he tried to deliberately recall what had actually happened, the details scattered. He couldn't hold the narrative together.

The triggers accumulated. A colleague mentioned needing a colonoscopy, and Marcus felt his shoulders lock, his breath catch. The smell of hand sanitizer in the staff bathroom sent him out of the building. A student's parent came to his office smelling faintly of alcohol—perhaps from the night before—and Marcus's hands shook so badly he had to grip the desk. He wasn't sure why that particular smell terrified him; perhaps it was bound up with hospital waiting rooms, with the helplessness of watching others fall apart. Each trigger seemed to confirm what he'd already decided: that his body was unreliable, that he couldn't trust himself to manage even the simplest interaction. So he rehearsed more, avoided more, isolated further.

Marcus finally called a therapist in June, after his superintendent expressed concern about his increasingly withdrawn behavior and erratic attendance at administrative meetings. He sat in the waiting room of the clinic—a place that, mercifully, smelled like coffee and old carpet, not antiseptic—and told the therapist that he didn't know who he was anymore. He was terrified that he'd never work through this, that the person he'd been was gone for good. What he wanted most was to feel like himself again, to trust his body and his mind. What frightened him most was that he'd already tried so hard to protect himself through isolation and control, and it had only made him feel more alone.
